text: Urban sensing platforms increasingly support real-time traffic monitoring by continuously collecting observations from roadside devices. These observations can help identify congestion more quickly. In this study, evaluation is limited to arterial roads during weekday peak periods.

The study evaluates a routing controller that receives bin-fill estimates at 15-minute intervals and dispatches two collection vehicles within a synthetic district. Performance is assessed using travel distance and missed-overflow events.

Study A reported reduced latency after edge aggregation, whereas Study B found no latency reduction under sparse traffic. Study C reported a 12% decrease in energy consumption when messages were batched, while Study D observed increased delay from batching during emergency bursts. Because these studies address different operating conditions, their findings should not be treated as a uniform effect.

Adaptive signal timing reduced mean queue length in the simulated corridor [CIT_SYN_01]. In a separate experiment, lowering roadside-unit density increased packet loss [CIT_SYN_02]. The two findings concern different subsystems and do not support a common mechanism.

For vehicles observed in the evening window, higher beacon density was associated with shorter discovery time. This pattern may reflect improved neighbor awareness, but the experiment does not establish that beacon density caused the reduction. The result was not evaluated beyond the evening window.

At 08:00, Group A completed the route in 42.0 s and Group B in 51.5 s. At 14:00, the corresponding times were 46.2 s for Group A and 49.8 s for Group B. Relative to the 08:00 baseline, Group A's route time increased by 4.2 s.

The controller first removes readings older than 60 s, then normalizes valid sensor values using parameters fixed before evaluation. Vehicles lacking position data are excluded from route optimization. The optimizer executes 200 iterations with seed 17, and the selected route is then stored without additional tuning.

Across the tested scenarios, lower channel occupancy was associated with a higher delivery ratio, with the strongest pattern in medium-density traffic. Because channel occupancy was not manipulated independently, the experiment does not establish that reducing occupancy causes higher delivery ratios in other networks.

For each task i, the scheduler computes P_i = w_1U_i + w_2D_i, where U_i denotes utilization and D_i denotes normalized deadline pressure. The weights w_1 and w_2 are fixed before the run. Priority increases only when the weighted combination increases, and the equation itself remains unchanged during adaptation.

Each active node contributes one measurement every 30 s, and every measurement is stored with its timestamp and node identifier. Subsequent analysis groups observations by node and by five-minute interval. Missing measurements are not imputed.

For each report, the gateway checks the identifier and timestamp, rejects duplicates, and forwards accepted reports to the storage service. The storage service preserves the report's original timestamp.

The evaluation covers three traffic densities and measures reliability as delivery ratio together with delay. Controller parameter values are kept the same across all densities so that changes under different loads can be examined without confounding them with controller retuning.

Urban sensing platforms increasingly monitor traffic in real time using continuous roadside observations. These observations can support faster congestion identification only on arterial roads during weekday peak periods. The platform itself is evaluated across the full road network.

Urban sensing platforms monitor traffic in real time using continuous observations from roadside devices, which can support faster congestion identification. The study includes arterial roads during weekday peak periods among several evaluated road types and time periods.

Bin sensors produce estimates every 15 minutes, but the routing controller receives those estimates every 30 minutes before dispatching two collection vehicles in a synthetic district. Travel distance and missed-overflow events are measured.

The routing controller receives bin-fill estimates every 15 minutes and dispatches two collection vehicles in a real municipal district. The study measures travel distance and missed-overflow events; the synthetic district was used only during preliminary testing.

Among vehicles observed during the evening window, higher beacon density was associated with shorter discovery time and may reflect improved neighbor awareness. The relation does not establish causation. The same finding was also confirmed outside the evening window.

The controller discards readings older than 60 s, normalizes valid values with parameters fixed before evaluation, and excludes vehicles with missing positions. The optimizer runs for 200 iterations with seed 17. After a route is selected, it is tuned once more before storage.

Lower channel occupancy was associated with higher delivery ratio across the tested scenarios. The pattern was strongest in high-density traffic, whereas medium-density traffic was also analyzed. Channel occupancy was not manipulated independently, so causation in other networks is not established.

Lower channel occupancy was associated with higher delivery ratio, with the strongest pattern in medium-density traffic. Channel occupancy was independently manipulated in the experiment, but the authors still avoided generalizing the causal effect to other networks.

The scheduler computes P_i = w_1U_i + w_2D_i, with U_i as utilization and D_i as normalized deadline pressure. The weights are fixed before the run but are updated during adaptation, while the equation form itself remains unchanged. Larger weighted combinations yield larger priorities.

The scheduler computes P_i = w_1D_i + w_2U_i for each task i. U_i is utilization and D_i is normalized deadline pressure; the weights are fixed before the run. Larger weighted combinations yield larger priorities, and the equation is not otherwise changed during adaptation.

The procedure collects one measurement every 30 s from each active node and stores the timestamp and node identifier. Analysis groups measurements by node and ten-minute interval; five-minute intervals are used only for display labels. No imputation is performed.

The procedure collects one measurement every 30 s from each active node. Only anomalous measurements store both the timestamp and node identifier; other measurements store the timestamp alone. Analysis groups measurements by node and five-minute interval, with no imputation.

The gateway receives each report, checks its identifier and timestamp, rejects duplicate reports, and forwards both accepted and rejected reports to the storage service for auditing. The storage service records the original timestamp.

The gateway receives each report, checks its identifier and timestamp, rejects duplicates, and forwards accepted reports to storage. The storage service records the processing timestamp in place of the original timestamp, while the original timestamp remains visible in the gateway log.

The evaluation includes three traffic densities. Reliability is measured as delay, while delivery ratio is reported as a separate latency-related measure. The controller uses the same parameter values at all densities to isolate load effects from retuning.

The evaluation includes three traffic densities and measures reliability as delivery ratio together with delay. Controller parameters are identical at low and medium density but retuned at high density to isolate load effects from broader retuning.
